title: Cyber incident lessons from Equiniti and ICE
seoTitle: Cyber incident lessons from Equiniti and Intercontinental Exchange
excerpt: Two SEC settlements test separate cyber duties: protect client assets during an intrusion and notify regulators on time. These cases do not establish a wider enforcement trend.
content:
## Two cases, two distinct control duties

Two Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) settlements illustrate different cyber-related duties for financial-market firms. The Equiniti matter concerns protection of client securities and funds from theft or misuse. The Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) matter concerns timely notification to the SEC after a potential intrusion. Together they support practical questions for boards and control owners, but two cases cannot establish a wider enforcement trend.

On 20 August 2024, the SEC announced settled charges against Equiniti Trust Company LLC, formerly American Stock Transfer & Trust Company LLC. The SEC said Equiniti failed to assure that client securities and funds were protected against theft or misuse. The failures led to losses of client funds in two separate cyber intrusions in 2022 and 2023. The SEC's order also imposed an $850,000 penalty. [Read the SEC order against Equiniti](https://www.sec.gov/files/litigation/admin/2024/34-100780.pdf).

On 22 May 2024, the SEC announced that ICE agreed to pay a $10 million penalty to settle charges concerning nine wholly owned subsidiaries, including the New York Stock Exchange. The order said ICE caused the subsidiaries to fail to inform the SEC in a timely way about a cyber intrusion, as required by Regulation Systems Compliance and Integrity (Regulation SCI). The SEC order says a third party warned ICE in April 2021 of a potential system intrusion. The issue described is the reporting obligation; it is not evidence that late reporting caused the intrusion. [Read the SEC order concerning ICE and its subsidiaries](https://www.sec.gov/files/litigation/admin/2024/34-100206.pdf).

## Translate the cases into control tests

The Equiniti settlement makes safeguarding the central test. A firm should be able to show who can access customer securities and funds, how unusual activity is detected, and how response teams limit customer exposure while investigating an intrusion. Examples of relevant evidence include access reviews, alert-to-case records, incident timelines, reconciliation results, customer impact assessments, and documented remediation. These are practical control tests derived from the case, not a claim that the SEC prescribed this exact evidence list.

The ICE settlement makes the path from detection to regulatory notification the central test. A firm should be able to trace an alert from the technical team to the person responsible for assessing reporting duties, show how the decision and timing were recorded, and demonstrate how the route works when several subsidiaries share systems or incident responders. Useful evidence includes the incident log, escalation matrix, decision record, notification timeline, and results of a scenario exercise. The point is to test whether the reporting chain works under pressure, not to infer unreported facts about ICE.

These duties are related but not interchangeable. A firm may contain an incident yet fail to notify a regulator promptly; it may notify a regulator and still need to establish whether client property was adequately protected. Management should therefore test the asset-protection response and the reporting route as separate outcomes, while ensuring they draw on a common, accurate incident timeline.

## Practical questions for a board or risk committee

1. In the last exercise, could the firm reconstruct the timeline from first alert through containment, customer impact assessment, decision ownership and any regulatory notification?
2. Can control owners show evidence that access to customer property was reviewed and that unusual activity alerts were investigated and closed?
3. Do the incident plan and reporting matrix name decision-makers, deputies, deadlines and routes for each relevant legal entity?
4. Has the firm tested an incident that begins with a third-party warning, rather than an alert generated by its own monitoring?
5. Are lessons from exercises and real events assigned to named owners, tracked to closure and retested?

These are RegActions analysis questions, not legal advice or a statement of regulator-mandated wording.

## Key Takeaways

* Test client-asset safeguards separately from cyber incident containment; retain access-review, alert-investigation and reconciliation evidence.
* Exercise the full notification chain from technical detection to a documented regulatory decision, including subsidiary hand-offs.
* Preserve one incident timeline that supports both customer-impact assessment and any required notification.
* Use third-party warnings in scenario testing; do not assume the first signal will come from internal monitoring.
* Assign exercise findings to owners, set completion evidence and retest remediated controls.

## About the Data

This brief uses two unique SEC source records concerning Equiniti and ICE. They are dated 22 May 2024 to 20 August 2024. Both describe settled SEC charges and verified penalties, with two distinct USD penalty amounts. The period refers to the publication dates of the SEC actions; the underlying incidents occurred earlier. The brief is limited to these two cases and does not measure cyber enforcement across the wider market.
